clue.text: Aesthetic realm gets one close to being in convulsions

indicators.note: being in tells us one piece sits inside the word for convulsions

parts.note: convulsions are fits, sudden seizures
close to means near

explanation.surface: Someone drawn into the world of aesthetics finds it drives them close to convulsions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being in' is the container signal. 'gets one' reads in the surface as a person getting close; the I it suggests is already in the convulsions word, so those words add no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Painting, sculpture and similar creative disciplines make up the domain of beauty and taste.

clue.text: Having the enemy in to complete a quartet?

definitions.text: Having the enemy in to complete a quartet?

parts.words: Having the enemy in to complete a quartet?
parts.note: 'the enemy' is time, as in 'time is the enemy'; adding time to length, breadth and height completes a set of four

explanation.walkthrough: 'The enemy' is the well-worn phrase for time; physics adds time as a fourth axis to the three of space.
explanation.definitionFit: Spacetime has three spatial axes plus time, making a four-part framework.

clue.text: Children's character in an odd yarn

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A children's storybook figure turns up in a peculiar tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the letters spanning 'aN ODD Yarn'.
explanation.definitionFit: The little wooden boy with a bell on his hat is a classic figure from Enid Blyton's children's books.

clue.text: Dog given an outing before something at the pub

indicators.note: before puts the first piece ahead of the second

parts.note: an idea given an outing has been aired
ale is a drink served at the pub

explanation.surface: A dog taken for a walk ahead of a visit to the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A large terrier breed from Yorkshire is an example of a dog.

clue.text: Case put in article by accountant

indicators.note: by means next to, so the second piece follows the first

parts.note: the definite article
CA is a chartered accountant

explanation.surface: A legal case written up in an article by an accountant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' is not a lawsuit but a sheath, a botanical or anatomical term.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology a sheath or capsule enclosing an organ or spores is called this.

clue.text: Sheep facing each other in the grass

indicators.note: two animals facing each other means one copy of the word is turned round to face the other

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: Two sheep stand nose to nose in the grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'facing each other' is the reversal signal: picture two sheep nose to nose, so one copy of the word reads backwards against the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A coarse coastal species planted to stabilise sand dunes is a kind of grass.

clue.text: A couple of females, wanting particular bloke, quarrel

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female, so two of them give FF
Ray is a man's name, standing for one particular bloke

explanation.surface: Two women both wanting the same man leads to a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A public brawl or fight is a legal term for a disturbance of the peace.

clue.text: Parliamentarian circle needing leader

parts.note: a circle is a round shape
a head is a leader, as of a school

explanation.surface: A political circle in need of someone to lead it.
explanation.walkthrough: In the English Civil War the Parliament side were nicknamed for their close-cropped hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Supporters of Parliament against Charles I in the Civil War bore this nickname.

clue.text: Queen I entertain at 'ome, surprisingly

indicators.note: surprisingly signals the letters before it are arranged in an unexpected new order

explanation.surface: A queen says she will host a party at her house, much to everyone's surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: ''ome' is home with the H dropped, Cockney style, giving OME to the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The wife of Louis XVI was the last queen of France before the Revolution.

clue.text: A pierrot playing in a foreign capital

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are performing in a different arrangement

explanation.surface: A clown in white performs abroad in some capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges A PIERROT.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the administrative seat of South Africa, so a capital outside Britain.

clue.text: Two foreign articles we put on are not English pants and vest?

parts.note: un is the French indefinite article, der the German definite one
un is the French indefinite article, der the German definite one
taken as written

indicators.note: E is English, and not means it is left out of the word that comes before

explanation.surface: Puzzling over two foreign items of clothing that we wear, which are not called pants and vest in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not English' drops the E from ARE, leaving AR. The question mark flags that pants and vest are just examples.
explanation.definitionFit: Briefs and a singlet are examples of clothes worn next to the skin.

clue.text: Mineral — something powdery that gets mixed inside

indicators.note: only the middle of the word is stirred, so one inner letter shifts its place

parts.note: flour is a fine powdery substance

explanation.surface: A mineral powder that gets stirred in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets mixed inside' swaps the inner O and U of FLOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an old name for fluorite, a calcium fluoride mineral.

clue.text: Dull commercial? You need a nymph!

parts.note: a dry speech is dull
an ad is a commercial

explanation.surface: An advert so boring that only a nymph could save it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth a tree spirit is a type of nymph.

clue.text: How the jockey wants to be? Starts with the rider getting into a seat

definitions.text: How the jockey wants to be?

indicators.note: getting into puts those letters inside the other piece

parts.note: a saddle is a seat, so with 'a' this gives A SADDLE

indicators.note: the starts of the words 'the' and 'rider' are taken

explanation.surface: A jockey's aim, beginning with the rider climbing into the saddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts with' gives T and R; 'getting into' puts them after the S of A SADDLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider sits with legs either side of the horse, astride it.

clue.text: Preachy types, mean people holding interview as a test

indicators.note: holding says one piece contains the other

parts.note: misers are stingy, mean people
an oral is a spoken exam, an interview used as a test

explanation.surface: Sanctimonious people and skinflints put a candidate through a grilling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' is the container signal. 'mean' looks like a verb in the surface but is the adjective stingy.
explanation.definitionFit: People who lecture others on right and wrong are sanctimonious lecturers.

clue.text: Amaretto's surprisingly served with this food!

indicators.note: surprisingly signals the letters of the word before are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is startled that almond liqueur is served alongside a dinner dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' rearranges AMARETTOS; the possessive 's here supplies an S.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef or lamb cooked in the oven is a typical Sunday dish.

clue.text: Group reportedly calm in well-rehearsed manoeuvre

parts.note: a set is a group

indicators.note: reportedly means we hear the word rather than see it

parts.note: peace is calm

explanation.surface: A group is said to be calm while carrying out a practised move.
explanation.definitionFit: In football, a corner or free kick routine planned in training is such a move.

clue.text: Founder of state revealed by half the flags

indicators.note: half the word means only its first four of eight letters are used

parts.note: pennants are long tapering flags

explanation.surface: A state's founder is shown on half the flags flying.
explanation.walkthrough: William Penn, a Quaker, founded the American state of Pennsylvania.
explanation.definitionFit: The English Quaker granted land by Charles II established Pennsylvania.

clue.text: Man trapped under ridiculously rigid frame

indicators.note: in a down entry, being trapped under means placed below, so it comes last
ridiculously signals that the letters of the word after are rearranged

parts.note: Ron is a man's name

explanation.surface: A man pinned beneath a rigid frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ridiculously' rearranges RIGID to GRIDI, and RON goes beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: A grill of parallel bars for cooking is this kind of metal grating.

clue.text: Floater taking limited number — gosh!

parts.note: no. is the shortened form of number
ah is an exclamation like gosh

explanation.surface: A boat taking only a few passengers, to everyone's surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floater' is not a buoy but the man who built the Ark and floated it, a playful word for him.
explanation.definitionFit: The Biblical patriarch who built the Ark rode out the Flood afloat.

clue.text: The hissing wireless?

parts.note: an old valve radio set that hisses, as if powered by a boiler

explanation.walkthrough: Wireless is the old British word for a radio; the phrase is a jokey name for traditional radio as opposed to television.
explanation.definitionFit: Old-fashioned sound broadcasting is nicknamed this, as if it ran on boilers.

clue.text: Coloured rod with fish on

parts.note: cray is short for crayfish
taken as written

explanation.surface: A painted fishing rod with a fish hooked on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rod' suggests fishing, but it is a stick of coloured wax.
explanation.definitionFit: A wax drawing stick used by children is a coloured rod.

clue.text: Forbid international arrangement for credit

indicators.note: an arrangement of the word credit puts its letters in a new order

explanation.surface: Banning an international deal for credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangement for' rearranges CREDIT to ERDICT.
explanation.definitionFit: To prohibit formally is the verb sense of a legal ban.

clue.text: Beat and energy evident in this dance

parts.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
go means energy or vigour

explanation.surface: Rhythm and vigour shown in a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A passionate Argentine ballroom number is an example of a dance.

clue.text: Foster maybe to admit what he didn't quite do!

parts.note: Doctor Foster of the nursery rhyme, so DR is the doctor
to own up is to admit

explanation.surface: Getting Foster to confess something he nearly did.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Foster went to Gloucester, stepped in a puddle 'right up to his middle', and nearly went under; the definition leans on the rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme the doctor fell into a deep puddle, almost dying under water.

clue.text: Marks on script made by old boy, a priest

parts.note: OB is short for old boy, a former pupil
Eli was the priest who raised Samuel in the Bible

explanation.surface: Notes on a manuscript written by a former pupil who is now a priest.
explanation.walkthrough: These are the dagger-like signs used in old manuscripts to mark doubtful passages.
explanation.definitionFit: Daggers or division-like signs annotating spurious text in ancient manuscripts are such marks.

clue.text: Poor journalist, being captured by French soldier!

indicators.note: being captured by says one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: Michel Ney was Napoleon's marshal
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A poor reporter taken prisoner by a French trooper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being captured by' is the container signal. Marshal Ney was one of Napoleon's best-known commanders, a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking money or the basics of life describes someone in want.

clue.text: In harmony with study by fellow covering winter sport

parts.note: to con is to study, as in conning a text

indicators.note: covering says one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: a gent is a fellow
RU is rugby union, played in the British winter

explanation.surface: Agreeing with research by a man who writes about winter sports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covering' is the container signal. Rugby union is played through the British winter, which is why it counts as a winter sport here.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in agreement or correspondence is to be consistent, matching.

clue.text: The French red wine that's undiscovered

parts.note: la is French for the
tent is a dark red Spanish wine

explanation.surface: A French red wine that nobody has found yet.
explanation.walkthrough: TENT is a sweet dark Spanish red, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hidden, present but not yet showing, is dormant.

clue.text: Agree to have something tossed for decision, then throw of dice

parts.note: a coin is tossed to decide

indicators.note: a throw of the dice scatters them in a new order

explanation.surface: Settling an agreement by tossing a coin and then rolling dice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'throw of' rearranges DICE to CIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: To correspond exactly, match up, is to agree in timing or position.
